claim: Small micromere cells arise from an asymmetric cleavage of the micromeres at the embryonic fifth cleavage.
source: Small micromere cells arise from an asymmetric cleavage of the micromeres at the embryonic fifth cleavage (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pehrson and Cohen, 1986 and reference to Figure 1A showing the developmental stages.

claim: The small micromeres divide once within the vegetal plate to produce eight cells.
source: These cells divide once within the vegetal plate to produce eight cells (Pehrson and Cohen, 1986).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pehrson and Cohen, 1986.

claim: The eight small micromeres migrate along with the growing archenteron during gastrulation until they reach the animal pole.
source: The eight small micromeres migrate along with the growing archenteron during gastrulation until they reach the animal pole (Yajima and Wessel, 2012; Campanale et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Yajima and Wessel, 2012 and Campanale et al., 2014.

claim: Post-migration, the small micromeres incorporate into the coelomic pouches, which are found on either side of the developing esophagus.
source: Post-migration, the small micromeres incorporate into the coelomic pouches, which are found on either side of the developing esophagus (Hyman, 1955; Pehrson and Cohen, 1986; Luo et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hyman, 1955; Pehrson and Cohen, 1986; and Luo et al., 2012.

claim: The coelomic pouches specification is initiated early in development by Delta/Notch signaling.
source: Their specification is initiated early in development by Delta/Notch signaling (Sherwood and McClay, 1999; Sweet et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to Sherwood and McClay, 1999 and Sweet et al., 2002.

claim: Only those small micromeres that reach the left coelomic pouch, which will become the future adult rudiment, will survive until adulthood.
source: Only those small micromeres that reach the left coelomic pouch, which will become the future adult rudiment, will survive until adulthood.
evidence: This is stated directly in the text as an observation about small micromere fate.

claim: During metamorphosis of the indirect developing sea urchin, the embryonic small micromeres incorporate into the adult rudiment's left somatocoel.
source: During metamorphosis of the indirect developing sea urchin, the embryonic small micromeres incorporate into the adult rudiment's left somatocoel, which will later give rise to the gonads of the adult animal and possibly other tissues (Hyman, 1955).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hyman, 1955.

claim: The adult rudiment's left somatocoel will later give rise to the gonads of the adult animal and possibly other tissues.
source: During metamorphosis of the indirect developing sea urchin, the embryonic small micromeres incorporate into the adult rudiment's left somatocoel, which will later give rise to the gonads of the adult animal and possibly other tissues (Hyman, 1955).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hyman, 1955 and includes speculation about other tissues.

claim: Previous research has suggested that the small micromeres contribute to the adult PGCs.
source: Previous research has suggested that the small micromeres contribute to the adult PGCs; however, it has not been shown directly whether the small micromeres contribute to additional adult tissues or whether the only source of the adult PGCs are the small micromeres (Pehrson and Cohen, 1986; Voronina et al., 2008; Juliano et al., 2010a; Juliano et al., 2010b; Yajima and Wessel, 2010; Yajima and Wessel, 2012; Wessel et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: It has not been shown directly whether the small micromeres contribute to additional adult tissues or whether the only source of the adult PGCs are the small micromeres.
source: Previous research has suggested that the small micromeres contribute to the adult PGCs; however, it has not been shown directly whether the small micromeres contribute to additional adult tissues or whether the only source of the adult PGCs are the small micromeres (Pehrson and Cohen, 1986; Voronina et al., 2008; Juliano et al., 2010a; Juliano et al., 2010b; Yajima and Wessel, 2010; Yajima and Wessel, 2012; Wessel et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge, supported by citations.

claim: The possibility remains that the small micromeres go on to produce multiple cell types including, but not limited to PGCs.
source: The possibility remains that the small micromeres go on to produce multiple cell types including, but not limited to PGCs (Yajima and Wessel, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yajima and Wessel, 2015.

claim: During gut invagination, the small micromeres did not change position relative to the adjacent mesoderm cells of the advancing archenteron.
source: In Yajima et al., it was observed that during gut invagination, the small micromeres did not change position relative to the adjacent mesoderm cells of the advancing archenteron.
evidence: This is a description of observations from Yajima et al.

claim: Once small micromeres reach the tip of the archenteron, they must actively migrate to the left and right coelomic pouches.
source: It was concluded that once they reach the tip of the archenteron, the small micromeres must actively migrate to the left and right coelomic pouches (Yajima and Wessel, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yajima and Wessel, 2012.

claim: Campanale et al. described an active migration throughout gastrulation and post-gastrulation as small micromeres make their way to the coelomic pouch.
source: Seemingly contradictory evidence from Campanale et al. described an active migration throughout gastrulation and post-gastrulation as they make their way to the coelomic pouch (Campanale et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Campanale et al., 2014.

claim: Small micromeres are autonomous and active while migrating throughout gastrulation when removed from their endogenous location and placed ectopically.
source: When removed from their endogenous location and placed ectopically, we find that the small micromeres are autonomous and active while migrating throughout gastrulation to make it 'home' to the coelomic pouch.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the authors' experiments.

claim: The active motility of small micromeres during gastrulation is essential for ectopic small micromeres to undergo directed 'homing' migration to the coelomic pouch.
source: Their active motility during gastrulation is essential for the ectopic small micromeres to undergo directed 'homing' migration to the coelomic pouch.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the authors' experimental observations.

claim: A specific subcircuit composed of Pax6, Six3, Six1/2, Eya, and Dach1 is responsible for the directed homing mechanism of small micromeres.
source: An assay using the robust homing potential of these cells reveals a 'coherent feed-forward' transcriptional subcircuit composed of Pax6, Six3, Six1/2, Eya, and Dach1 that is responsible for the directed homing mechanism of these multipotent progenitors.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the authors' experiments using the homing assay.

claim: The linkages of the homing subcircuit are strikingly similar to a circuit involved in retinal specification in Drosophila.
source: The linkages of that circuit are strikingly similar to a circuit involved in retinal specification in Drosophila suggesting that systems-level tasks can be highly conserved even though the tasks drive unrelated processes in different animals.
evidence: This is a comparative analysis and interpretation by the authors.

claim: Systems-level tasks can be highly conserved even though the tasks drive unrelated processes in different animals.
source: The linkages of that circuit are strikingly similar to a circuit involved in retinal specification in Drosophila suggesting that systems-level tasks can be highly conserved even though the tasks drive unrelated processes in different animals.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the similarity between the homing circuit and the retinal determination circuit.

claim: Small micromeres actively changed shape throughout gastrulation until they reach the tip of the archenteron.
source: Small micromeres actively changed shape throughout gastrulation (extend filopodia and lamellipodia) until they reach the tip of the archenteron.
evidence: This is supported by Figure 1C and Video 1 showing time-lapse imaging of small micromere behavior.

claim: Small micromeres extend filopodia and lamellipodia throughout gastrulation.
source: Small micromeres actively changed shape throughout gastrulation (extend filopodia and lamellipodia) until they reach the tip of the archenteron.
evidence: This is supported by Figure 1C and Video 1 showing cellular behavior.

claim: Throughout invagination of the archenteron, the small micromeres were highly active.
source: As seen in Figure 1C and Video 1, throughout invagination of the archenteron, the small micromeres were highly active.
evidence: This is supported by Figure 1C and Video 1.

claim: Small micromeres underwent many cell shape changes, blebbing, and pseudopodia extensions during archenteron invagination.
source: They underwent many cell shape changes, blebbing, and pseudopodia extensions as was also seen by Campanale et al.
evidence: This is supported by the authors' observations and citation to Campanale et al.

claim: Small micromeres extended filopodia and lamellipodia through the basal lamina surrounding the archenteron.
source: They extended filopodia and lamellipodia through the basal lamina surrounding the archenteron.
evidence: This is an observation from the authors' experiments.

claim: Small micromeres retained an adhesion and were not displaced relative to the adjacent invaginating epithelial cells during archenteron invagination.
source: Nevertheless, they retained an adhesion and were not displaced relative to the adjacent invaginating epithelial cells (Figure 1C and Video 1, 12 hr 00 min–18 hr 00 min).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 1C and Video 1.

claim: When gastrulation was completed at 20 hpf (early prism stage), small micromere behavior changed in tandem with a change in the basal lamina.
source: When gastrulation was completed at 20 hpf (early prism stage), small micromere behavior changed in tandem with a change in the basal lamina.
evidence: This is an observation from the authors' experiments.

claim: At the end of gastrulation, the basal lamina was undergoing remodeling, with large gaps in the laminin component of the basement membrane at the tip of the archenteron.
source: At a time corresponding to the end of gastrulation, laminin immunostaining indicated that the basal lamina was undergoing remodeling, as there were large gaps in the laminin component of the basement membrane at the tip of the archenteron (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 2A showing laminin immunostaining.

claim: Small micromeres delaminated through gaps in the basal lamina at the tip of the archenteron.
source: Through those gaps, the small micromeres delaminated (Figure 2A), moved to the blastocoelar side of the remodeling basal lamina, and then actively migrated to the posterior end of the left or right coelomic pouch where they were then re-enveloped with a basal lamina layer by 2 dpf (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 2A showing the delamination process.

claim: Small micromeres actively migrated to the posterior end of the left or right coelomic pouch after delamination.
source: Through those gaps, the small micromeres delaminated (Figure 2A), moved to the blastocoelar side of the remodeling basal lamina, and then actively migrated to the posterior end of the left or right coelomic pouch where they were then re-enveloped with a basal lamina layer by 2 dpf (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 2B showing the final location.

claim: Small micromeres were re-enveloped with a basal lamina layer by 2 dpf after reaching the coelomic pouch.
source: Through those gaps, the small micromeres delaminated (Figure 2A), moved to the blastocoelar side of the remodeling basal lamina, and then actively migrated to the posterior end of the left or right coelomic pouch where they were then re-enveloped with a basal lamina layer by 2 dpf (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 2B showing laminin surrounding the small micromeres.

claim: The migratory behavior of the small micromeres suggested that they underwent an EMT at the beginning of their migratory phase.
source: The migratory behavior of the small micromeres suggested that they underwent an EMT at the beginning of their migratory phase over the archenteron and to their coelomic pouch.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on observed cellular behaviors.

claim: Small micromeres de-adhered, breached a basal lamina, changed shape, actively migrated within the blastocoel, and then rejoined an epithelium, demonstrating EMT and possibly MET properties.
source: These cells de-adhered, breached a basal lamina, changed shape, actively migrated within the blastocoel, and then rejoined an epithelium, demonstrating a number of EMT, and perhaps mesenchymal–epithelial transition (MET), properties.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed cellular behaviors.

claim: Ectopically placed small micromeres underwent an EMT coincident with the endogenous EMT event of the skeletogenic cells.
source: Ectopically placed small micromeres underwent an EMT coincident with the endogenous EMT event of the skeletogenic cells.
evidence: This is supported by Figure 2C,D showing laminin staining at the time of ingression.

claim: Laminin is absent both at the site of skeletogenic cell ingression and at the site of ectopic small micromere ingression.
source: Laminin (red) is absent both at the site of skeletogenic cell ingression (indicated by white arrows at the site of ingression) and at the site of ectopic small micromere (SM, green) ingression (indicated by a yellow arrow).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 2C,D showing laminin immunostaining.

claim: Micromeres placed at the vegetal pole homed 86.6% of the time (n = 213).
source: Donors placed in the endogenous location homed 86.6% (n = 213) of the time (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is quantitative data from the homing assay shown in Figure 3A.

claim: 13.4% of observed cases where micromeres were placed at the vegetal pole were considered 'no homing' because fluorescent small micromeres could not be found in the host embryo's coelomic pouch.
source: 13.4% of observed cases that were considered 'no homing' were instances where we could not find fluorescent small micromeres in the host embryo's coelomic pouch.
evidence: This is quantitative data from the homing assay.

claim: Micromeres placed ectopically at the equator homed 93.7% of the time (n = 74).
source: Micromeres were then placed ectopically between the Veg1 and Veg2 tier and in the animal half between the An1 and An2 tier of presumptive ectodermal cells (scored together as equator), at the animal pole, or in the blastocoel. No matter where they were placed, the vast majority of small micromeres transplanted to ectopic positions anywhere in the embryo made it home (Equator = 93.7% (n = 74), Animal Pole = 78.6% (n = 11), Blastocoel = 78.6% (n = 11)) (Figure 3B–D).
evidence: This is quantitative data from the homing assay shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Micromeres placed ectopically at the animal pole homed 78.6% of the time (n = 11).
source: Micromeres were then placed ectopically between the Veg1 and Veg2 tier and in the animal half between the An1 and An2 tier of presumptive ectodermal cells (scored together as equator), at the animal pole, or in the blastocoel. No matter where they were placed, the vast majority of small micromeres transplanted to ectopic positions anywhere in the embryo made it home (Equator = 93.7% (n = 74), Animal Pole = 78.6% (n = 11), Blastocoel = 78.6% (n = 11)) (Figure 3B–D).
evidence: This is quantitative data from the homing assay shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Micromeres placed ectopically in the blastocoel homed 78.6% of the time (n = 11).
source: Micromeres were then placed ectopically between the Veg1 and Veg2 tier and in the animal half between the An1 and An2 tier of presumptive ectodermal cells (scored together as equator), at the animal pole, or in the blastocoel. No matter where they were placed, the vast majority of small micromeres transplanted to ectopic positions anywhere in the embryo made it home (Equator = 93.7% (n = 74), Animal Pole = 78.6% (n = 11), Blastocoel = 78.6% (n = 11)) (Figure 3B–D).
evidence: This is quantitative data from the homing assay shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The majority of transplants were scored to be in the left coelomic pouch after homing.
source: Interestingly, the majority of transplants were scored to be in the left coelomic pouch after homing suggesting a survival mechanism to ensure the proposed primordial germ cells make it onto adulthood to contribute to the gamete pool.
evidence: This is an observation from the homing assay data.

claim: The ectopic small micromeres arrived independently of the endogenous micromeres.
source: We then assayed at intervals up to 24 hpf and saw that the ectopically placed micromeres arrived independently of the endogenous micromeres (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B showing independent arrival.

claim: The transplanted small micromeres remained at the ectopic site until the primary mesenchyme cells (PMCs) ingressed.
source: The transplanted small micromeres remained at the ectopic site until the primary mesenchyme cells (PMCs) ingressed.
evidence: This is an observation from time-lapse experiments.

claim: At 9–10 hpf, the ectopic small micromeres ingressed into the blastocoel at the time of skeletogenic cell ingression.
source: At that time (9–10 hpf), the ectopic small micromeres also ingressed into the blastocoel (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 2C,D showing the timing of ingression.

claim: Isolated small micromeres can ingress on their own, independent of large micromeres.
source: By ectopically transplanting just 32-cell stage small micromeres (as opposed to the usual 16-cell stage micromere, which would result in large and small micromere cells) (Figure 2C), we observed the small micromeres autonomously invade through the laminin layer independent of large micromeres.
evidence: This is supported by Figure 2C showing isolated small micromere transplants.

claim: The ectopic small micromeres breached the laminin layer at the same time as the PMC EMT.
source: The ectopic small micromeres breached the laminin layer (Figure 2D, yellow arrow) at the same time as the PMC EMT (Figure 2D, white arrows) suggesting that the small micromeres create the hole through which they breach and invade, even though the endogenous small micromeres actually breach the basement membrane about 6–8 hr later when they leave the tip of the archenteron.
evidence: This is supported by Figure 2D showing laminin staining.

claim: The small micromeres create the hole through which they breach and invade the basement membrane.
source: The ectopic small micromeres breached the laminin layer (Figure 2D, yellow arrow) at the same time as the PMC EMT (Figure 2D, white arrows) suggesting that the small micromeres create the hole through which they breach and invade, even though the endogenous small micromeres actually breach the basement membrane about 6–8 hr later when they leave the tip of the archenteron.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that ectopic small micromeres breach the laminin layer.

claim: The endogenous small micromeres breach the basement membrane about 6–8 hr later than ectopic small micromeres when they leave the tip of the archenteron.
source: The ectopic small micromeres breached the laminin layer (Figure 2D, yellow arrow) at the same time as the PMC EMT (Figure 2D, white arrows) suggesting that the small micromeres create the hole through which they breach and invade, even though the endogenous small micromeres actually breach the basement membrane about 6–8 hr later when they leave the tip of the archenteron.
evidence: This is an observation about the timing difference between ectopic and endogenous small micromeres.

claim: Delta was knocked down in host embryos to test if mesoderm is the lineage to which the small micromeres home.
source: First, to ask if the mesoderm is the lineage to which the small micromeres home, we knocked out Delta, a signal necessary for mesodermal specification (Sherwood and McClay, 1999; Sweet et al., 2002).
evidence: This is an experimental approach described by the authors, with citations supporting Delta's role.

claim: The lack of mesoderm had an effect on homing.
source: The lack of mesoderm, indeed, had an effect on homing.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the Delta knockdown experiment.

claim: When Delta was knocked down in host embryos, control micromeres did not home to any significant location in the embryo 65% of the time (n = 23, p < 0.0001).
source: The small micromeres did not home to any significant location in the embryo (coelomic pouches were non-existent in the KD) and became lost in the blastocoelar space as is seen in cases we deemed 'no homing' 65% of the time (n = 23, p < 0.0001) (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is quantitative data from the Delta knockdown experiment shown in Figure 4C.

claim: 35% of the time in Delta knockdown experiments, there was an incomplete knockdown resulting in a coelomic pouch and the small micromeres homed to that location.
source: 35% of the time, there was an incomplete knockdown of the Delta signal resulting in a coelomic pouch and the small micromeres homed to that location.
evidence: This is an observation from the Delta knockdown experiment.

claim: FoxC is expressed in both the oral coelomic pouch mesoderm and the small micromeres.
source: FoxC is expressed in both the oral coelomic pouch mesoderm and the small micromeres; however, only when it was perturbed in the small micromere did it affect homing, and only 26% (n = 19, p < 0.001) of the time did the small micromeres successfully make it to the coelomic pouch (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by expression data and the homing assay shown in Figure 5A.

claim: FoxC affects small micromere homing when knocked down in the micromere, with only 26% (n = 19, p < 0.001) of small micromeres successfully reaching the coelomic pouch.
source: FoxC is expressed in both the oral coelomic pouch mesoderm and the small micromeres; however, only when it was perturbed in the small micromere did it affect homing, and only 26% (n = 19, p < 0.001) of the time did the small micromeres successfully make it to the coelomic pouch (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is quantitative data from the FoxC knockdown experiment shown in Figure 5A.

claim: FoxC knockdown in the mesoderm had no inhibitory effect on homing (n = 13).
source: FoxC is expressed in both the oral coelomic pouch mesoderm and the small micromeres; however, only when it was perturbed in the small micromere did it affect homing, and only 26% (n = 19, p < 0.001) of the time did the small micromeres successfully make it to the coelomic pouch (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is data from the FoxC knockdown experiment shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Dach1 affected homing when knocked down in the mesoderm (n = 10, p < 0.0001) but did not affect homing when perturbed in the small micromere (n = 13).
source: Dach1, an aboral mesoderm transcription factor, affected homing when knocked down in the mesoderm (n = 10, p < 0.0001) but did not affect homing when perturbed in the small micromere (n = 13).
evidence: This is quantitative data from the Dach1 knockdown experiment shown in Figure 5B.

claim: When control micromeres were transplanted to a Dachshund1 morpholino perturbed host, the control small micromeres were only able to home in 10% (n = 10, p < 0.0001) of scored cases.
source: When control micromeres were transplanted to a Dachshund1 morpholino perturbed host, the control small micromeres were only able to home in 10% (n = 10, p < 0.0001) of scored cases (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is quantitative data from the Dach1 knockdown experiment shown in Figure 5B.

claim: When Dach1 was knocked down in the small micromeres only, and the host embryo was a control, homing ability was scored as successful in 77% of cases.
source: In contrast, when Dach1 was knocked down in the small micromeres only, and the host embryo was a control, homing ability was scored as successful in 77% of cases.
evidence: This is quantitative data from the Dach1 knockdown experiment.

claim: Dach1 is necessary in the targeted tissue for homing to occur.
source: We concluded that Dach1 was necessary in the targeted tissue for homing to occur.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the Dach1 knockdown experiments.

claim: When control micromeres were transplanted to a Pax6 knockdown host, the small micromeres were only able to home 40% (n = 10, p < 0.004) of the time.
source: When control micromeres were transplanted to a Pax6 knockdown host, the small micromeres were only able to home 40% (n = 10, p < 0.004) of the time (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is quantitative data from the Pax6 knockdown experiment shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Six3 affected homing when knocked down in the mesoderm (n = 9, p < 0.00009) but had no effect on homing when perturbed only in the small micromere (n = 9).
source: Aboral mesoderm transcription factor, Six3 affected homing when knocked down in the mesoderm (n = 9, p < 0.00009) but had no effect homing when perturbed only in the small micromere (n = 9).
evidence: This is quantitative data from the Six3 knockdown experiment shown in Figure 5D.

claim: When control micromeres were transplanted to a Six3 knockdown host, the small micromeres were able to home 11% (n = 9, p < 0.00009) of scored cases.
source: When control micromeres were transplanted to a Six3 knockdown host, the small micromeres were able to home 11% (n = 9, p < 0.00009) of scored cases (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is quantitative data from the Six3 knockdown experiment shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Eya affected homing when knocked down in the mesoderm (n = 7, p < 0.002) but did not affect homing when perturbed in the small micromeres (n = 8).
source: Aboral transcriptional co-activator, Eya, affected homing when knocked down in the mesoderm (n = 7, p < 0.002) but did not affect homing when perturbed in the small micromeres (n = 8).
evidence: This is quantitative data from the Eya knockdown experiment shown in Figure 5E.

claim: When control micromeres were transplanted to an Eya knockdown host, small micromeres were able to home 28.5% of the time (n = 7, p < 0.002).
source: When control micromeres were transplanted to an Eya knockdown host, small micromeres were able to home 28.5% of the time (n = 7, p < 0.002) (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is quantitative data from the Eya knockdown experiment shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Six1/2 affected homing when knocked down in the mesoderm (n = 17, p < 0.02) and did not affect homing when knocked down in the micromere (n = 11).
source: Aboral transcription factor, Six1/2, affected homing when knocked down in the mesoderm, as well (n = 17, p < 0.02) and did not affect homing when knocked down in the micromere (n = 11).
evidence: This is quantitative data from the Six1/2 knockdown experiment shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Control micromeres transplanted to a Six1/2 knockdown host were able to home 65% (n = 17, p < 0.02) of scored cases.
source: Control micromeres transplanted to a Six1/2 knockdown host were able to home 65% (n = 17, p < 0.02) of scored cases (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is quantitative data from the Six1/2 knockdown experiment shown in Figure 5F.

claim: The Six1/2 effect on homing is modest, but statistically significant relative to controls within that experiment.
source: This effect is modest, but statistically significant relative to controls within that experiment.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the statistical significance of the Six1/2 knockdown data.

claim: Transcription factors FoxF, SoxE, FoxC, and Pitx2 did not appear necessary for homing when perturbed in the coelomic pouch mesoderm.
source: Transcription factors FoxF, SoxE, FoxC, and Pitx2 did not appear necessary for homing when perturbed in the coelomic pouch mesoderm (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 1 showing no effect on homing.

claim: When the same knockdowns are stained for endogenous vasa expression, small micromeres are still able to reach the coelomic pouches.
source: It is important to note that when the same knockdowns are stained for endogenous vasa expression (labeling the small micromeres), small micromeres are still able to reach the coelomic pouches (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 2 showing vasa expression in knockdowns.

claim: The control endogenous small micromeres are within the coelomic pouches in tight clusters.
source: We observe that the control endogenous small micromeres are within the coelomic pouches in tight clusters (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A) while the knockdowns exhibit various levels of disorganization (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B–H).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 2A showing control vasa expression.

claim: The knockdown small micromeres exhibit various levels of disorganization compared to controls.
source: We observe that the control endogenous small micromeres are within the coelomic pouches in tight clusters (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A) while the knockdowns exhibit various levels of disorganization (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B–H).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 2B–H showing vasa expression in knockdowns.

claim: Since the endogenous small micromeres normally home over a very short distance, the knockdown small micromeres remain close to the coelomic pouches.
source: Since the endogenous small micromeres normally home over a very short distance, the knockdown small micromeres, as might be expected, remain close to the coelomic pouches—they do not disperse from that vicinity, but they do not tightly cluster in the correct location.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the vasa expression data in knockdowns.

claim: At the time of vasa staining, there is prevalent cell rearrangement at the tip of the archenteron that leads to the fusion of the oral ectoderm and foregut endoderm.
source: Also, at this time, there is prevalent cell rearrangement at the tip of the archenteron that leads to the fusion of the oral ectoderm and foregut endoderm (unpublished observations).
evidence: This is an observation from unpublished data.

claim: Of the eleven genes screened for homing behavior, only six were necessary for homing.
source: Thus of the eleven genes screened for homing behavior, only six were necessary for homing.
evidence: This is a summary of the homing assay results.

claim: Each of the five transcription factors involved in controlling homing is expressed in the aboral coelomic pouch.
source: Each of the five transcription factors involved in controlling homing is expressed in the aboral coelomic pouch.
evidence: This is a summary of expression data for the homing transcription factors.

claim: Transcription factors Dach1, Eya, Six1/2, and Pax6 are co-localized in the aboral coelomic pouch.
source: Luo and Su showed that transcription factors Dach1, Eya, Six1/2, and Pax6 are co-localized in the aboral coelomic pouch (Luo et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Luo et al., 2012.

claim: Six3 was found to be expressed in the aboral mesoderm early in development.
source: Six3 was found to be expressed in the aboral mesoderm early in development, and by double fluorescent in situ hybridization, we see six3 to also overlap with aboral marker, eya (Figure 6B) (Wei et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 6B showing double fluorescent in situ hybridization and citation to Wei et al., 2011.

claim: Six3 overlaps with aboral marker, eya.
source: Six3 was found to be expressed in the aboral mesoderm early in development, and by double fluorescent in situ hybridization, we see six3 to also overlap with aboral marker, eya (Figure 6B) (Wei et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 6B showing double fluorescent in situ hybridization.

claim: Six3 was seen to be tightly apposed with vasa expression but is exclusive from small micromeres.
source: Six3 was seen to be tightly apposed with vasa expression but is exclusive from small micromeres.
evidence: This is supported by Figure 6A showing double fluorescent in situ hybridization.

claim: Six3 expression is distinct from the oral, myosin, domain of expression.

source: Luo and Su also noted that transcription factors Dach1 and FoxC are expressed in the oral coelomic pouch (Luo et al., 2012).

claim: During gastrulation, dach1 is found throughout and at the tip of the archenteron in the presumptive coelomic pouch cells.
source: During gastrulation, it is found throughout and at the tip of the archenteron in the presumptive coelomic pouch cells (A5-8) and is maintained in that tissue and gut throughout coelomic pouch coalescence with the small micromeres at the pluteus stage (A7-8).

claim: Six3's earliest detectable expression is at early blastula.
source: six3's earliest detectable expression is at early blastula (B1).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 6—figure supplement 1 showing six3 expression time course.

claim: Six3 is found in the animal pole region, and expression in the coelomic pouch mesoderm begins around mesenchyme blastula.
source: It is found in the animal pole region, and expression in the coelomic pouch mesoderm begins around mesenchyme blastula (B3).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 6—figure supplement 1 showing six3 expression time course.

claim: Throughout gastrulation, six3 is found in the apical plate domain and the future coelomic pouch cells.
source: Throughout gastrulation, six3 is found in the apical plate domain and the future coelomic pouch cells (B3-4).

claim: The six3 apical domain of expression is responsible for giving rise to neural fates.

claim: Post-gastrulation, six3 is expressed in both coelomic pouches.

claim: Eya begins expression at mid-gastrula in the aboral coelomic pouch at the tip of the archenteron.
source: eya begins expression at mid-gastrula in the aboral coelomic pouch at the tip of the archenteron (D4).

claim: Eya expression by 32 hpf is found in the left coelomic pouch.
source: eya expression by 32 hpf is found in the left coelomic pouch (D8).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 6—figure supplement 1 showing eya expression time course.

claim: Pax6 expression begins at mid to late gastrula stage in the aboral coelomic pouch at the tip of the archenteron, roughly at the time of ectopic small micromere homing.
source: pax6 expression begins at mid to late gastrula stage in the aboral coelomic pouch at the tip of the archenteron, roughly at the time of ectopic small micromere homing (E5), and by 32 hpf is found in the left coelomic pouch and two lateral patches of ectoderm presumed to be neural in fate (E8).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 6—figure supplement 1 showing pax6 expression time course.

claim: By 32 hpf, pax6 is found in the left coelomic pouch and two lateral patches of ectoderm presumed to be neural in fate.
source: pax6 expression begins at mid to late gastrula stage in the aboral coelomic pouch at the tip of the archenteron, roughly at the time of ectopic small micromere homing (E5), and by 32 hpf is found in the left coelomic pouch and two lateral patches of ectoderm presumed to be neural in fate (E8).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 6—figure supplement 1 showing pax6 expression time course.

claim: The co-localization of the five transcription factors in the coelomic pouches and temporal expression patterns suggest that these transcription factors may be interacting.
source: By surveying this gene set, we conclude that their co-localization in the coelomic pouches and temporal expression patterns suggest that these transcription factors may be interacting (diagram, Figure 6D).
evidence: This is an inference based on expression data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: When Dach1 was perturbed using a morpholino specific to the start of translation, an increased expression of dach1 was seen, indicating self repression.
source: When Dach1 was perturbed using a morpholino specific to the start of translation, we saw by in situ hybridization an increased expression of dach1 (indicating self repression).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 7 showing in situ hybridization results.

claim: The upregulation of dach1 seen in the gut was a result of dach1 self-repression not only in the gut but also later in the coelomic pouch mesoderm expression.
source: Knowing that dach1 is expressed in the endoderm earlier in development from our time course data, we concluded that the upregulation seen in the gut was a result of dach1 self-repression not only in the gut but also later in the coelomic pouch mesoderm expression.
evidence: This is an inference based on expression time course data and perturbation results.

claim: A down-regulation of six3 and a down-regulation of eya transcripts was seen in the Dach1 perturbation.
source: A down-regulation of six3 and a down-regulation of eya transcripts was also seen in the Dach1 perturbation.
evidence: This is supported by Figure 7 showing in situ hybridization results.

claim: Dach1 positively regulates six3 and eya and inhibits the overexpression of itself by repression.
source: These data indicate that Dach1 positively regulates six3 and eya and inhibits the overexpression of itself by repression (Figure 7).
evidence: This is an inference based on the perturbation results shown in Figure 7.

claim: When Six3 was perturbed using a start site morpholino, a self up-regulation of six3 was seen but only in the apical expression domain.
source: When Six3 was perturbed using a start site morpholino, we saw a self up-regulation of six3 but only in the apical expression domain, a down-regulation of eya, and a down-regulation of pax6 transcripts.
evidence: This is supported by Figure 7 showing in situ hybridization results.

claim: Six3 perturbation caused a down-regulation of eya and a down-regulation of pax6 transcripts.
source: When Six3 was perturbed using a start site morpholino, we saw a self up-regulation of six3 but only in the apical expression domain, a down-regulation of eya, and a down-regulation of pax6 transcripts.
evidence: This is supported by Figure 7 showing in situ hybridization results.

claim: Six3 positively regulates eya and pax6 in the coelomic pouch mesoderm.
source: We conclude from these data that Six3 positively regulates eya and pax6 in the coelomic pouch mesoderm.
evidence: This is an inference based on the Six3 perturbation results.

claim: Perturbing Eya showed a down-regulation of six3, six1/2, and a self-down-regulation of eya.
source: Perturbing Eya in the same way showed a down-regulation of six3, six1/2, and a self-down-regulation of eya.
evidence: This is supported by Figure 7 showing in situ hybridization results.

claim: Eya positively regulates itself, six3, and six1/2 by co-acting with Six1/2.
source: Knowing that Eya is a transcriptional co-activator of Six1/2, Eya must positively regulate itself, six3, and six1/2 by co-acting with Six1/2.
evidence: This is an inference based on the Eya perturbation results and knowledge of Eya's function.

claim: Six1/2 perturbation caused regulatory interactions that reflected those found in the Eya knockdowns indicating that Eya and Six1/2 act synergistically.
source: Next, Six1/2 was perturbed, and, as expected, regulatory interactions found reflected those found in the Eya knockdowns indicating that Eya and Six1/2 do, in fact, act synergistically as has been seen before (Heanue et al., 1999; Materna et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by the perturbation results and citations to Heanue et al., 1999 and Materna et al., 2013.

claim: Pax6 perturbation caused down-regulation of six3, eya, and itself.
source: Finally, Pax6 perturbation caused down-regulation of six3, eya, and itself.
evidence: This is supported by Figure 7 showing in situ hybridization results.

claim: Pax6 positively regulates six3, eya, and itself.
source: Pax6, therefore, positively regulates six3, eya, and itself (Figure 7).
evidence: This is an inference based on the Pax6 perturbation results shown in Figure 7.

claim: When the network was laid out in a Biotapestry model, the subcircuit controlling the homing mechanism was readily discerned as a coherent feed-forward loop composed of multiple feedback loops.
source: When the network was laid out in a Biotapestry model, the subcircuit controlling the homing mechanism was readily discerned as a coherent feed-forward loop composed of multiple feedback loops that sustain its robust nature (Figure 8A) (Longabaugh et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 8A showing the Biotapestry network model and citation to Longabaugh et al., 2005.

claim: The Pax-Six-Eya-Dach RDGN is necessary for specification of retinal cell types in many systems.
source: The Pax-Six-Eya-Dach RDGN is necessary for specification of retinal cell types in many systems (Purcell et al., 2005; Kozmik et al., 2007; Kumar, 2009; Salzer et al., 2010; Weasner and Kumar, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The same five factors contribute to a coherent feed-forward circuit for Drosophila eye specification.
source: The same five factors contribute to a coherent feed-forward circuit for Drosophila eye specification (Kumar, 2009) (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 8B showing the Drosophila eye circuit and citation to Kumar, 2009.

claim: Few linkages between the eye and small micromere homing circuits are different.
source: Few linkages between the eye and small micromere homing circuits are different (Figure 8).
evidence: This is a comparative analysis shown in Figure 8.

claim: Small micromeres home with high fidelity to the coelomic pouches no matter where they initially are placed in the embryo.
source: Our chimera experiments show that small micromeres home with high fidelity to the coelomic pouches no matter where they initially are placed in the embryo.
evidence: This is a summary of the chimera experiment results.

claim: Small micromere homing utilizes an autonomous EMT and a directed movement to the target site in the coelomic pouch.
source: That homing utilizes an autonomous EMT and a directed movement to the target site in the coelomic pouch.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the experimental observations.

claim: Perturbation analysis identified the transcriptional inputs upstream of the putative homing signal.
source: Perturbation analysis identified the transcriptional inputs upstream of the putative homing signal.
evidence: This is a summary of the perturbation analysis results.

claim: Network analysis of the transcription factors necessary for homing signal production unveiled a stereotypical coherent feed-forward subcircuit that controls the attractive signal.
source: Network analysis of the transcription factors necessary for homing signal production unveiled a stereotypical coherent feed-forward subcircuit that controls the attractive signal.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the network analysis.

claim: The same subcircuit is present and used for another purpose in Drosophila.
source: That the same subcircuit is present and used for another purpose in Drosophila was an unexpected outcome.
evidence: This is a comparative observation by the authors.

claim: Deployment of the same subcircuit in the two organisms for two very different purposes suggests that ancient subcircuit functions necessary for systems-level operations in networks may be employed as a unit as new networks evolve.
source: While it is possible that the similarity is due to convergent evolution, deployment of the same subcircuit in the two organisms for two very different purposes also suggests another possibility. Ancient subcircuit functions necessary for systems-level operations in networks may be employed as a unit as new networks evolve rather than build new systems level operations gene by gene.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: It isn't yet known whether evolution favors subcircuits of similar topology moving as a unit to perform similar functions in diverse cell types.
source: It isn't yet known whether evolution favors subcircuits of similar topology moving as a unit to perform similar functions in diverse cell types, but advances in systems-level studies should reveal the frequency of this phenomenon.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge and future directions.

claim: Normally small micromeres retain an adhesion to adjacent cells during archenteron extension.
source: The data from the chimera experiments show that normally small micromeres retain an adhesion to adjacent cells during archenteron extension.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the chimera experiments.

claim: When small micromeres arrive at the tip of the archenteron, they leave the epithelium using an EMT through a laminin-containing basement membrane.
source: When they arrive at the tip of the archenteron, they then leave the epithelium using an EMT through a laminin-containing basement membrane, migrate to the posterior end of the coelomic pouch, and transition back to an epithelium as they coalesce with the coelomic pouch.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the experimental observations.

claim: Small micromeres migrate to the posterior end of the coelomic pouch after leaving the epithelium.
source: When they arrive at the tip of the archenteron, they then leave the epithelium using an EMT through a laminin-containing basement membrane, migrate to the posterior end of the coelomic pouch, and transition back to an epithelium as they coalesce with the coelomic pouch.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the experimental observations.

claim: Small micromeres transition back to an epithelium as they coalesce with the coelomic pouch.
source: When they arrive at the tip of the archenteron, they then leave the epithelium using an EMT through a laminin-containing basement membrane, migrate to the posterior end of the coelomic pouch, and transition back to an epithelium as they coalesce with the coelomic pouch.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the experimental observations.

claim: Ectopically placed small micromeres behave differently from the endogenous small micromeres in that they fail to retain epithelial adhesions through gastrulation.
source: Ectopically placed small micromeres behave differently from the endogenous small micromeres in that they fail to retain epithelial adhesions through gastrulation and instead go through an EMT at the time PMCs ingress.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the ectopic transplant experiments.

claim: Ectopically placed small micromeres go through an EMT at the time PMCs ingress.
source: Ectopically placed small micromeres behave differently from the endogenous small micromeres in that they fail to retain epithelial adhesions through gastrulation and instead go through an EMT at the time PMCs ingress.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the ectopic transplant experiments.

claim: There must be a non-autonomous cue to keep the endogenous small micromeres in place during gastrulation.
source: The fact that the ectopically placed small micromeres lose adhesion and go through EMT independent of the timing of archenteron tip formation implies that there must be a non-autonomous cue to keep the endogenous small micromeres in place during gastrulation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the difference in behavior between endogenous and ectopic small micromeres.

claim: Without a local cue, the small micromeres actively home from the beginning of gastrulation as seen with the behavior of ectopically placed small micromeres.
source: Without that local cue, the small micromeres actively home from the beginning of gastrulation as seen with the behavior of ectopically placed small micromeres.
evidence: This is an inference based on the behavior of ectopically placed small micromeres.

claim: There must be a non-autonomous signal that is recognized by small micromeres when they reach the tip of the forming archenteron that cues them to initiate the EMT and migration.
source: Further, there must be a non-autonomous signal that is recognized by small micromeres when they reach the tip of the forming archenteron that cues them to initiate the EMT and migration.
evidence: This is an inference based on the timing of EMT in endogenous small micromeres.

claim: The behavior of the ectopic cells suggest that the migratory capacity can be activated at the beginning of gastrulation.
source: The behavior of the ectopic cells suggest that the migratory capacity can be activated at the beginning of gastrulation, but since they normally do not move from the epithelium until at the tip of the archenteron, another event may stimulate them to complete their journey to the coelomic pouches.
evidence: This is an inference based on the behavior of ectopic small micromeres.

claim: Since endogenous small micromeres normally do not move from the epithelium until at the tip of the archenteron, another event may stimulate them to complete their journey to the coelomic pouches.
source: The behavior of the ectopic cells suggest that the migratory capacity can be activated at the beginning of gastrulation, but since they normally do not move from the epithelium until at the tip of the archenteron, another event may stimulate them to complete their journey to the coelomic pouches.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed behavior.

claim: Observations of ectopically placed small micromeres reveal that the cells undergo directed cell migration to get to the coelomic pouch mesoderm.
source: Observations of ectopically placed small micromeres also reveal that the cells undergo directed cell migration to get to the coelomic pouch mesoderm.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the ectopic transplant experiments.

claim: The cells find their way to the coelomic pouch no matter their starting location.
source: The cells find their way to the coelomic pouch no matter their starting location.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the ectopic transplant experiments.

claim: Small micromeres appear to take a fairly direct route to their eventual target no matter where they are initially placed.
source: Small micromeres appear to take a fairly direct route to their eventual target no matter where they are initially placed.
evidence: This is an observation from the ectopic transplant experiments.

claim: Since the normal route involves movement through part of the blastocoel, and since ectopic small micromeres also use the blastocoelar route, the putative homing signal likely is produced earlier than the end of gastrulation.
source: Since the normal route involves movement through part of the blastocoel, and since ectopic small micromeres also use the blastocoelar route, the putative homing signal likely is produced earlier than the end of gastrulation since the ectopic small micromeres move through the blastocoel to the correct target well before gastrulation is completed.
evidence: This is an inference based on the timing of ectopic small micromere migration.

claim: At present, it is only speculation that there is a chemoattraction mechanism at play.
source: At present, it is only speculation that there is a chemoattraction mechanism at play.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge.

claim: If it were chemoattraction, the cue must work at the individual cell level since single small micromeres respond to the cue when ectopically placed.
source: If it were chemoattraction, the cue must work at the individual cell level since single small micromeres respond to the cue when ectopically placed.
evidence: This is a conditional inference based on the behavior of single ectopic small micromeres.

claim: The transcriptional regulation upstream of the putative signal offers approaches for its identification.
source: The transcriptional regulation upstream of that putative signal offers approaches for its identification.
evidence: This is a statement about future research directions.

claim: As an alternative hypothesis, the coelomic pouch NSM could be drawing the small micromeres to their final site by filopodia.
source: Potentially, as an alternative hypothesis, the coelomic pouch NSM could be drawing the small micromeres to their final site by filopodia, since it is known that these cells as well as the small micromeres extend filopodia (Hardin, 1988; Campanale et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an alternative hypothesis supported by citations to Hardin, 1988 and Campanale et al., 2014.

claim: The goal of determining upstream transcriptional regulation of the homing process requires connection of the homing network to chemoattraction mechanisms directly responsible for the directing migration.
source: The goal of determining upstream transcriptional regulation of the homing process requires connection of the aforementioned network (Figure 8A) to chemoattraction mechanisms (both attractant and repulsion) directly responsible for the directing migration.
evidence: This is a statement about future research directions.

claim: Other subcircuits are necessary to drive the EMT, for reception of the putative signal, and for directed movement in response.
source: In addition, other subcircuits are necessary to drive the EMT, for reception of the putative signal, and for directed movement in response.
evidence: This is an inference about the complexity of the regulatory network.

claim: Transcriptional control of directed cell migration is not well studied at a systems level.
source: Transcriptional control of directed cell migration is not well studied at a systems level.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of the field.

claim: Findings in the tunicate, Ciona intestinalis, describe the distinct transcriptional regulation of a cellular module that drives migration of heart precursors.
source: Findings in the tunicate, Ciona intestinalis, describe the distinct transcriptional regulation of a cellular module that drives migration of heart precursors. The heart GRN drives membrane protrusions and RhoGTPase signaling, tail retraction, adhesion, and polarity (Christiaen et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Christiaen et al., 2008.

claim: In Ciona heart cells, the cells constitutively expressed many of the factors required for cell behaviors, and it only took one or two factors to be under direct control of the developmental GRN to regulate the timing, directionality, onset, and termination of the heart cell precursors' journey.
source: One important feature of that study was that the cells constitutively expressed many of the factors required for these cell behaviors. It only took one or two factors to be under direct control of the developmental GRN to regulate the timing, directionality, onset, and termination of the heart cell precursors' journey.
evidence: This is a description of findings from the Ciona study.

claim: In the sea urchin, five different GRN subcircuits were shown to drive five different cellular components of an EMT.
source: In the sea urchin, five different GRN subcircuits were shown to drive five different cellular components of an EMT (Saunders and McClay, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Saunders and McClay, 2014.

claim: It is highly likely that the sea urchin developmental GRN will control directly expression of only a fraction of the proteins used for de-adhesion, motility, invasion of the basement membrane, altered cell polarity, and cell shape changes, while many other proteins in those processes will be constitutively expressed.
source: It is highly likely, like Ciona heart cells, that the sea urchin developmental GRN will control directly expression of only a fraction of the proteins used for de-adhesion, motility, invasion of the basement membrane, altered cell polarity, and cell shape changes, all components of an EMT, while many other proteins in those processes will be constitutively expressed.
evidence: This is an inference based on the Ciona example and sea urchin EMT studies.

claim: Using small micromere homing as an assay, the authors were able to begin to unravel the intricacy of GRN subcircuits that control cell migration to a target site.
source: Using small micromere homing as an assay, we were able to begin to unravel the intricacy of GRN subcircuits that control cell migration to a target site.
evidence: This is a summary of the authors' work.

claim: This work demonstrates how morphogenesis can be controlled by conserved specification GRN subcircuits.
source: This work thus demonstrates how morphogenesis can be controlled by conserved specification GRN subcircuits.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the authors' work.

claim: To accomplish the feat of small micromeres becoming associated with the aboral coelomic pouch, both the cells that home and the target cells must enact a series of coordinated, but independent processes.
source: The small micromere homing example reveals something else in morphogenetic movement control. We tend to think of the result of the movement: the small micromeres become associated with the aboral coelomic pouch through homing. Yet, to accomplish that feat, both the cells that home and the target cells must enact a series of coordinated, but independent processes.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the complexity of the homing process.

claim: A set of genes that control the production of the putative homing signal was found.
source: Here, we found a set of genes that control the production of the putative homing signal.
evidence: This is a summary of the authors' findings.

claim: Being that the subcircuit is of coherent feed-forward topology, it is suspected to be found at the most distal part of a larger GRN and will act downstream of the specification circuitry of the signal-producing cell type.
source: Being that the subcircuit is of coherent feed-forward topology, we suspect it will be found at the most distal part of a larger GRN; therefore, it will act downstream of the specification circuitry of the signal-producing cell type.
evidence: This is an inference based on the topology of the subcircuit.

claim: Connecting the upstream subcircuit to the downstream signal(s) will provide a tool for explaining one component of the homing mechanism that is known to be transcriptionally controlled.
source: Connecting that upstream subcircuit to the downstream signal(s) will provide a tool for explaining one component of the homing mechanism that we know to be transcriptionally controlled.
evidence: This is a statement about future research directions.

claim: Recognizable RDGN components are deployed in a variety of developmental processes in different organisms.
source: Recognizable RDGN components are deployed in a variety of developmental processes in different organisms.
evidence: This is a general statement supported by the examples that follow.

claim: Putative GRN models were constructed from published data on demosponge canal systems, vertebrate skeletal muscle, and mouse otic placodes.
source: After pooling published data from three different fields of study (demosponge canal systems, vertebrate skeletal muscle, and mouse otic placodes), we were able to construct putative GRN models (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 8—figure supplement 1 showing the putative GRN models.

claim: Although each respective subcircuit is embedded in a larger specification GRN, when extracted as a subcircuit, it appears that the RDGN feed-forward topology has been deeply conserved.
source: Although each respective subcircuit is embedded in a larger specification GRN, when extracted as a subcircuit, it appears that the RDGN feed-forward topology has been deeply conserved (Torres et al., 1996; Heanue et al., 1999; Relaix and Buckingham, 1999; Xu et al., 1999; Ridgeway and Skerjanc, 2001; Kardon et al., 2002; Laclef et al., 2003; Riley and Phillips, 2003; Zheng, 2003; Ozaki, 2004; Silver, 2004; Relaix et al., 2013; Rivera et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Only now that a complete RDGN subcircuit has been made in the sea urchin, can we hypothesize about what evolutionary mechanism may be at play.
source: Only now that we have been able to make a complete RDGN subcircuit in the sea urchin, can we hypothesize about what evolutionary mechanism may be at play.
evidence: This is a statement about the significance of the authors' work.

claim: With the same transcription factors involved in a similar feed-forward process in such a variety of tissues, the authors hypothesize that the RDGN subcircuit is ancient and has been repeatedly deployed as a unit to provide feed-forward control.
source: With the same transcription factors involved in a similar feed-forward process in such a variety of tissues, we hypothesize that the RDGN subcircuit is ancient and has been repeatedly deployed as a unit to provide feed-forward control.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: If this subcircuit is redeployed throughout evolution as a unit, the mechanism that keeps it intact is unknown.
source: If this subcircuit is redeployed throughout evolution as a unit, as seems to be the case given the frequency of its presence, the mechanism that keeps it intact is unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge.

claim: Evolving as a modular unit must mean that the subcircuit serves as an indispensible or important component in a network full of modular components.
source: Evolving as a modular unit must mean that the subcircuit serves as an indispensible or important component in a network full of modular components.
evidence: This is an inference about the evolutionary significance of the subcircuit.

claim: The assembly of the coherent feed-forward circuit, once established, appears to remain intact in separate lineages because that circuit must be critical for the GRNs in which it is embedded.
source: The assembly of the coherent feed-forward circuit, once established, appears to remain intact in separate lineages for the same reason: that circuit must be critical for the GRNs in which it is embedded.
evidence: This is an inference about the evolutionary conservation of the subcircuit.

claim: The presence of the RDGN subcircuit raises the question of whether there are other ancient or more recent subcircuits that have evolved as modules.
source: Its presence raises the question of whether there are other ancient or more recent subcircuits that have evolved as modules.
evidence: This is a question raised by the authors' findings.

claim: Since analysis of developmental GRNs is a relatively young field, it is possible that a number of ancient modular subcircuits evolve as units to assist in the diversification of cell types and morphogenesis.
source: Since analysis of developmental GRNs is a relatively young field, it is possible that a number of ancient modular subcircuits evolve as units to assist in the diversification of cell types and morphogenesis.
evidence: This is speculation about the broader implications of the findings.

claim: One obvious outcome of this mode of inheritance would be a contribution to robustness in developmental mechanisms.
source: One obvious outcome of this mode of inheritance would be a contribution to robustness in developmental mechanisms.
evidence: This is an inference about the functional significance of modular subcircuits.

claim: Once a subcircuit is particularly well integrated and suited for a given type of regulatory function, each of its members might act as a constraint on the others because any reduction in integration would be less adaptive.
source: And perhaps once a subcircuit is particularly well integrated and suited for a given type of regulatory function, each of its members (in our case, transcription factors) might act as a constraint on the others because any reduction in integration would be less adaptive.
evidence: This is speculation about the evolutionary constraints on subcircuit members.

claim: What is intriguing is how ancient the RDGN must be.
source: What is intriguing is how ancient the RDGN must be.
evidence: This is a statement about the evolutionary age of the RDGN.

claim: The RDGN is a circuit that is used because it efficiently provides an excellent feed-forward circuit that stabilizes the process to which it is attached.
source: It is a circuit that is used because it efficiently provides an excellent feed-forward circuit that stabilizes the process to which it is attached.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the functional significance of the RDGN.

claim: The RDGN is best studied in retinal determination but its ancestral role is unknown and could equally well be directed cell migration.
source: It is best studied in retinal determination but its ancestral role is unknown and could equally well be directed cell migration.
evidence: This is speculation about the ancestral function of the RDGN.
